¶
'''wicken''' (wik′n), ''n.'' [Appar. connected with ''wick''<sup>1</sup>, ''wicker''<sup>1</sup>, ''witch-elm'', etc.; but early forms have not been found.] The mountain-ash or rowan-tree, ''Pyrus Aucuparia.'' Also ''wicky.''

'''wicken-tree''' (wik′n-trē), ''n.'' Same as ''wicken.''

'''wicker'''<sup>1</sup> (wik′ėr), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [Also dial. ''wigger''; < ME. *''wiker'', ''wykyr''; cf. Sw. dial. ''vikker'', ''vekker'', ''vekare'', the sweet bay-leaved willow, = Dan. dial. ''vögger'', ''vegre'', also ''vöge'', a pliant rod, withy (''vögre-kurv'', ''vegre-kurv'', wicker-basket), ''væger'', ''vægger'', a willow; cf. Bav. dial. ''wickel'', bunch of tow on a distaff, G. ''wickel'', a roll; ult. < AS. ''wīcan'', etc., bend, yield: see ''wick''<sup>1</sup> and ''weak.''] '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A small pliant twig; an osier; a withe.
{{smaller block|Which hoops are knit as with ''wickers.''
{{right|''Wood'', Athenæ Oxon., I. (''Richardson.'')}}
For want of a pannier, spit your fish by the gills on a small ''wicker'' or such like.
{{right|''W. Lawson'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 197).}}
<poem>Aye wavering like the willow-''wicker'',
’Tween good and ill. ''Burns'', On Life.</poem>}}
'''2.''' Wickerwork in general; hence, an object made of this material, as a basket.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then quick did dress
His half milk up for cheese, and in a press
Of ''wicker'' press’d it. ''Chapman'', Odyssey, ix. 351.</poem>
<poem>Each [maiden] having a white ''wicker'', overbrimm’d
With April’s tender younglings. ''Keats'', Endymion, i.</poem>}}
'''3.''' A twig or branch used as a mark: same as ''wike''<sup>3</sup>.

'''II.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Consisting of wicker; especially, made of plaited twigs or osiers; also, covered with wickerwork: as, a ''wicker'' basket; a ''wicker'' chair.
{{smaller block|<poem>Robin Hood swam to a bush of broome,</poem>}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To twist (a thread) overmuch. ''Jamieson.'' [Scotch.]

'''wickered''' (wik′ėrd), ''a.'' [< ''wicker''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>] '''1.''' Made of wicker.—'''2.''' Covered with wickerwork.

'''wickerwork''' (wik′ėr-wėrk), ''n.'' Basketwork of any sort; anything plaited, woven, or wattled of flexible and tough materials, as osier, ratan, and shaved strips of wood.

'''wicket''' (wik′et), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wicket, wiket, wyket, viket'' = MD. ''wicket'', also ''wincket'', < OF. *''wiket, wisket, viquet, guichet'', F. ''guichet'' (Walloon ''wichet'') = Pr. ''guisquet'', a wicket; a dim. form, prob. ult. from the verb seen in AS. ''wīcan'', etc., give way: see ''wick''<sup>1</sup>, ''weak''.] '''1.''' A small gate or doorway, especially a small door or gate forming part of a larger one.
{{smaller block|<poem>When the buernes of the burgh were broght vpon slepe,
He [Sinon] warpit vp a ''wicket'', wan hom with-oute.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 11923}}
<poem>The clyket
That Januarie bar of the smale ''wyket''
By which into his gardyn ofte he wente.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Merchant’s Tale, l. 874}}
<poem>They steeked them a’ but a wee ''wicket'',
And Lammikin crap in.</poem>
{{right|''Lammikin'' (Child’s Ballads, III. 308)}}
<poem>“O, haste thee, Wilfrid!” Redmond cried;
“Undo that ''wicket'' by thy side!”</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Rokeby, v. 2}}}}

'''widdow†''', ''n.'' and ''v.'' An obsolete spelling of ''widow''<sup>1</sup>.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|wicked|6919|widdy}}</noinclude>ful; immoral; bad; wrong; iniquitous: a word of comprehensive signification, including everything that is contrary to the moral law, and applied both to persons and to their acts: as, a ''wicked'' man; a ''wicked'' deed; ''wicked'' ways; ''wicked'' lives; a ''wicked'' heart; ''wicked'' designs; ''wicked'' works.
{{smaller block|Thei ben fulle ''wykked'' Sarrazines and cruelle.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 112.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>To see this would deter a doubtful man
From mischievous intents, much more the practice
Of what is ''wicked''. ''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Malta, iv. 1.</poem>
Are men less ashamed of being ''wicked'' than absurd?
{{right|''Jon Bee'', Essay on Samuel Foote.}}}}
{{smaller block|To do an injury openly is, in his estimation, as ''wicked'' as to do it secretly, and far less profitable.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Machiavelli.}}}}
'''2†.''' Vile; baneful; pernicious; noxious.
{{smaller block|That wynde away the ''wicked'' ayer may hurle.
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 175.}}}}
{{smaller block|Faire Amorett must dwell in ''wicked'' chaines.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. ix. 24.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>As ''wicked'' dew as e’er my mother brush’d
With raven’s feather from unwholesome fen
Drop on you both. ''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 2. 321.</poem>}}
'''3†.''' Troublesome; difficult; hard; painful; unfavorable; disagreeable.

{{smaller block|Hony is the more swete yif mowthes have fyrst tasted savoures that ben ''wyckyd.'' {{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, iii. meter 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The wallis in werne ''wikked'' to assaile
With depe dikes and derke doubull of water.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1565.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>But this lande is full ''wicked'' to be wrought,
To hardde in hete, and over softe in weete.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 49.}}}}
{{smaller block|I pray, what ’s good, sir, for a ''wicked'' tooth? {{right|''Middleton (and others)'', The Widow, iv. 1.}}}}
'''4.''' Mischievous; prone or disposed to mischief, often good-natured mischief; roguish: as, a ''wicked'' urchin. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|Pen looked uncommonly ''wicked.'' {{right|''Thackeray'', Pendennis, xxvii.}}}}
{{smaller|'''The wicked one''', the devil.—'''Wicked Bible.''' See ''Bible.'' ='''Syn. 1.''' ''Illegal, Immoral'', etc. (see ''criminal''), ''Heinous, Infamous'', etc. (see ''atrocious''), unrighteous, profane, ungodly, godless, impious, unprincipled, vile, abandoned, profligate.}}

'''II.†''' ''n. sing.'' and ''pl.'' A wicked person; one who is or those who are wicked.
{{smaller block|Then shall that ''Wicked'' be revealed, whom the Lord shall consume. {{right|2 Thes. ii. 8.}}}}
{{smaller block|There lay his body vnburied all that Friday, and the morrow till afternoone, none daring to deliver his body to the sepulture; his head there ''wicked'' took, and, nayling thereon his hoode, they fixe it on a pole, and set it on London Bridge. {{right|''Stowe'', Annals (1605), p. 458.}}}}

'''wicked<sup>2</sup>''' (wik′ed), ''a.''   [< ''wick''<sup>3</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>, here merely an adj. extension.]   Quick; active. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|Another Irish woman of diminutive stature complacently described herself to a lady hiring her services as “small but ''wicked.''” {{right|''A. S. Palmer'', Folk-Etym., Int., p. xxii.}}}}

'''wickedly''' (wik′ed-li), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''wikkedly, wickedli, wikkedliche''; < ''wicked''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.]   In a wicked manner.

<poem>Ho keppit hym full kantly, kobbit with hym sore,
Woundit hym ''wickedly'' in hir wode angur.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 11025.}}}}

{{smaller block|I have sinned, and I have done ''wickedly''.
{{right|2 Sam. xxiv. 17.}}}}

'''wickedness''' (wik′ed-nes), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wikkednesse''; < ''wicked'' + ''-ness''. Cf. ME. ''wickenes'', ''wikenesse'', ''wiknes'', < ''wicke'' (see ''wick''<sup>7</sup>) + ''-ness''.]   '''1.''' Wicked character, quality, or disposition; depravity or corruption of heart; evil disposition; sinfulness: as, the ''wickedness'' of a man or of an action.

<poem>And al the ''wikkednesse'' in this worlde that man myȝt worche or thynke
Ne is no more to the mercye of God than in the see a glede.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), v. 291.}}}}

<poem>And after thi mercies that ben fele,
Lord, fordo my ''wickydnesse''.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 25.}}}}

{{smaller block|Goodness belongs to the Gods, Piety to Men, Revenge and ''Wickedness'' to the Devils. {{right|''Howell'', Letters, ii. 1.}}}}

'''2.''' Wicked conduct; evil practices; active immorality; vice; crime; sin.

{{smaller block|’Tis not good that children should know any ''wickedness''.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., ii. 2. 13.}}}}

<poem>There is a method in man’s ''wickedness'';
It grows up by degrees.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Beau. and Fl.''}}}}

'''3.''' A wicked thing or act; an act of iniquity.

{{smaller block|What ''wickedness'' is this that is done among you?
{{right|Judges xx. 12.}}}}

<poem>I’ll never care what ''wickedness'' I do
If this man come to good.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iii. 7. 99.}}}}

'''4.''' Figuratively, the wicked.
{{smaller block|<poem>Those tents thou sawest so pleasant were the tents
Of ''wickedness.''</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 60}}}}
='''Syn.''' Unrighteousness, villainy, rascality, knavery, atrocity, iniquity, enormity. See references under ''wicked.''

'''wicken''' (wik′n), ''n.''   [Appar. connected with ''wick''<sup>1</sup>, ''wicker''<sup>1</sup>, ''witch-elm'', etc.; but early forms have not been found.]   The mountain-ash or rowan-tree, ''Pyrus Aucuparia.'' Also ''wicky.''

'''wicken-tree''' (wik′n-trē), ''n.'' Same as ''wicken.''

'''wicker'''<sup>1</sup> (wik′ėr), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [Also dial. ''wigger''; < ME. *''wiker'', ''wykyr''; cf. Sw. dial. ''vikker'', ''vekker'', ''vekare'', the sweet bay-leaved willow, = Dan. dial. ''vögger'', ''vegre'', also ''vöge'', a pliant rod, withy (''vögre-kurv'', ''vegre-kurv'', wicker-basket), ''væger'', ''vægger'', a willow; cf. Bav. dial. ''wickel'', bunch of tow on a distaff, G. ''wickel'', a roll; ult. < AS. ''wīcan'', etc., bend, yield: see ''wick''<sup>1</sup> and ''weak.'']   '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A small pliant twig; an osier; a withe.
{{smaller block|Which hoops are knit as with ''wickers.''
{{right|''Wood'', Athenæ Oxon., I. (''Richardson.'')}}}}
{{smaller block|For want of a pannier, spit your fish by the gills on a small ''wicker'' or such like.
{{right|''W. Lawson'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 197).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Aye wavering like the willow-''wicker'',
’Tween good and ill. ''Burns'', On Life.</poem>}}
'''2.''' Wickerwork in general; hence, an object made of this material, as a basket.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then quick did dress
His half milk up for cheese, and in a press
Of ''wicker'' press’d it. ''Chapman'', Odyssey, ix. 351.</poem>
<poem>Each [maiden] having a white ''wicker'', overbrimm’d
With April’s tender younglings. ''Keats'', Endymion, i.</poem>}}
'''3.''' A twig or branch used as a mark: same as ''wike''<sup>3</sup>.

'''II.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Consisting of wicker; especially, made of plaited twigs or osiers; also, covered with wickerwork: as, a ''wicker'' basket; a ''wicker'' chair.
{{smaller block|<poem>Robin Hood swam to a bush of broome,</poem> The fryer to a ''wigger'' wand.
{{right|''Robin Hood and the Curtall Fryer'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 274).}}}}
{{smaller block|The lady was placed in a large ''wicker'' chair, and her feet wrapped up in flannel, supported by cushions.
{{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 266.}}}}
{{smaller block|The doll, seated in her little ''wicker'' carriage.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 40.}}}}
'''2.''' Made of flexible strips of shaved wood, ratan, or the like: as, ''wicker'' furniture; a ''wicker'' chair.

'''wicker<sup>1</sup>†''' (wik′ėr), ''v. t.''   [< ''wicker''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'']   To cover or fit with wickers or osiers; inclose in wickerwork.
{{smaller block|He looks like a musty bottle new ''wickered''.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man out of his Humour, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thir Ships of light timber, ''Wickerd'' with Oysier betweene, and coverd over with Leather, serv’d not therefore to tranceport them farr.
{{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., ii.}}}}

'''wicker<sup>2</sup>''' (wik′ėr), ''v.''   [Cf. ''wicker''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To twist, from being too tightly drawn.   ''Child’s Ballads'', Gloss.
{{smaller block|<poem>The nurice she knet the knot,
  And O she knet it sicker;
The ladie did gie it a twig [twitch],
  Till it began to ''wicker''.</poem>
{{right|''Laird of Wariestoun'' (Child’s Ballads, III. iii.).}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To twist (a thread) overmuch.   ''Jamieson.'' [Scotch.]

'''wickered''' (wik′ėrd), ''a.''   [< ''wicker''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>]   '''1.''' Made of wicker.—'''2.''' Covered with wickerwork.

'''wickerwork''' (wik′ėr-wėrk), ''n.'' Basketwork of any sort; anything plaited, woven, or wattled of flexible and tough materials, as osier, ratan, and shaved strips of wood.

'''wicket''' (wik′et), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wicket, wiket, wyket, viket'' = MD. ''wicket'', also ''wincket'', < OF. *''wiket, wisket, viquet, guichet'', F. ''guichet'' (Walloon ''wichet'') = Pr. ''guisquet'', a wicket; a dim. form, prob. ult. from the verb seen in AS. ''wīcan'', etc., give way: see ''wick''<sup>1</sup>, ''weak''.]   '''1.''' A small gate or doorway, especially a small door or gate forming part of a larger one.
{{smaller block|<poem>When the buernes of the burgh were broght vpon slepe,
He [Sinon] warpit vp a ''wicket'', wan hom with-oute.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 11923}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The clyket
That Januarie bar of the smale ''wyket''
By which into his gardyn ofte he wente.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Merchant’s Tale, l. 874}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>They steeked them a’ but a wee ''wicket'',
And Lammikin crap in.</poem>
{{right|''Lammikin'' (Child’s Ballads, III. 308)}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>“O, haste thee, Wilfrid!” Redmond cried;
“Undo that ''wicket'' by thy side!”</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Rokeby, v. 2}}}}

'''2†.''' A hole through which to communicate, or to view what passes without; a window, lookout, loophole, or the like.
{{smaller block|They have made barris to barre the dorys crosse weyse and they have made ''wykets'' on every quarter of the hws to schote owte atte, bothe with bowys and with hand-gunnys.
{{right|''Paston Letters'', I. 83.}}}}

'''3.''' A small gate by which the chamber of a canal-lock is emptied; also, a gate in the chute of a water-wheel, designed to regulate the amount of water passing to the wheel.—'''4.''' A half-high door.   ''E. H. Knight.''—'''5†.''' A hole or opening.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Wickettes'' two or three thou make hem couthe,
That yf a wicked worme oon holes mouthe
Besiege or stoppe, an other open be,
And from the wicked worme thus save thi bee.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 39.}}}}
'''6.''' In ''cricket:'' (''a'') The object at which the bowler aims, and before which, but a little on one side, the batsman stands. It consists of three stumps, having two bails lying in grooves along their tops. See ''cricket''<sup>2</sup> (with diagram).
{{smaller block|The ''wicket'' was formerly two straight thin battons called stumps, twenty-two inches high, which were fixed into the ground perpendicularly six inches apart, and over the top of both was laid a small round piece of wood called the bail. {{right|''Strutt'', Sports and Pastimes, p. 175.}}}}
{{smaller block|A desperate fight . . . between the drovers and the farmers with their whips and the boys with cricket-bats and ''wickets.'' {{right|''T. Hughes'', Tom Brown at Rugby, i. 4.}}}}
(''b'') A batsman’s tenure of his wicket. {{smaller|If the batting side pass their opponents’ full score with (say) six players to be put out, they are said to win “by six ''wickets''”—a colloquial abbreviation for “with six wickets to go down.”}} (''c'') The ground on which the wickets are set: as, play was begun with an excellent ''wicket.''—'''7.''' In ''coal-mining.'' See ''wicket-work.''

'''wicket-door''' (wik′et-dōr), ''n.'' A wicket.
{{smaller block|Through the low ''wicket-door'' they glide.
{{right|''Scott'', Rokeby, v. 29.}}}}

'''wicket-gate''' (wik′et-gāt), ''n.'' A small gate; a wicket.
{{smaller block|I am going to yonder ''wicket-gate'' before me.
{{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, i.}}}}

'''wicket-keeper''' (wik′et-kē″pėr), ''n.'' In ''cricket'', the player belonging to the fielding side who stands immediately behind the wicket to stop such balls as pass it. See diagram under ''cricket''<sup>2</sup>.
{{smaller block|“I’m your man,” said he. “''Wicket-keeper'', cover-point, slip, or long-stop—you bowl the twisters, I’ll do the fielding for you.” {{right|''Whyte Melville'', White Rose, II. xiii.}}}}

'''wicket-work''' (wik′et-wėrk), ''n.'' In ''coal-mining'', a variety of pillar and stall work sometimes adopted in the North Wales coal-field. {{smaller|The headings or stalls (called ''wickets'') are sometimes as much as 24 yards wide, and the pillars as much as 15. Two roadways are generally carried up each wicket.}}

'''wicking''' (wik′ing), ''n.''   [< ''wick''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ing''<sup>1</sup>.]   The material of which wicks are made, as in long pieces which can be cut at pleasure.
{{smaller block|Generally the traces of musk-cattle are in mass—like balls all melted together. . . . It struck me it would make capital ''wicking'' for Esquimaux lamps. {{right|''C. F. Hall'', Polar Expedition (1876), p. 161.}}}}

'''wickiup, wicky-up''' (wik′i-up), ''n.''   [Amer. Ind.]   An American Indian house or hut; especially, a rude hut, as of brushwood, such as is built by the Apaches and other low tribes: in distinction from the tepee of skins stretched on stacked lodge-poles. Wickiups are built on the spot as required, and are not moved.
{{smaller block|After an hour’s riding to the south, we came upon old Indian ''wicky-ups''. {{right|''Amer. Antiquarian'', XII. 205.}}}}

'''Wickliffite,''' ''a.'' and ''n.'' See ''Wyclifite''.

'''wick-trimmer''' (wik′trim″ėr), ''n.'' A pair of scissors or shears for trimming wicks; a pair of snuffers.

'''wicky''' (wik′i), ''n.''; pl. ''wickies'' (-iz).   [Cf. ''wicken.'']   '''1.''' Same as ''wicken.''—'''2.''' Same as ''sheep-laurel.''

'''wicky-up''', ''n.'' See ''wickiup.''

'''Wicliffite''', ''a.'' and ''n.'' See ''Wyclifite.''

'''wicopy''' (wik′ọ̄-pi), ''n.''   [Also ''wikop'', ''wicup'', ''wickup;'' of Amer. Ind. origin.]   '''1.''' The leatherwood, ''Dirca palustris.''—'''2.''' One of the willow-herbs, as ''Epilobium angustifolium'', ''E. lineare'', and perhaps other species: distinguished as ''Indian'' or ''herb wicopy.'' See ''willow-herb.''

'''wid''' (wid), ''prep.'' An obsolete or dialectal form of ''with''<sup>1</sup>.
{{smaller block|<poem>Sifter hole water same ez a tray,
Ef you fill it ''wid'' moss en dob it ''wid'' clay.</poem>
{{right|''J. C. Harris'', Uncle Remus, xxii.}}}}

'''widbin''' (wid′bin), ''n.''   [A dial. form of ''woodbine.'']   '''1.''' The woodbine, ''Lonicera Periclymenum.'' [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>The rawn-tree in [and] the ''widdbin''
Haud the witches on cum in.</poem>
{{right|''Gregor'', Folk-lore N. E. Scotland. (''Britten and Holland.'')}}}}
'''2.''' The dogwood, ''Cornus sanguinea.'' [Prov. Eng.]—'''Widbin pear-tree''', {{smaller|the whitebeam, ''Pyrus Aria.'' [Prov. Eng.]}}

'''widdershins†''' (wid′ėr-shinz), ''adv.'' See ''withershins.''

'''widdow†''', ''n.'' and ''v.'' An obsolete spelling of ''widow''<sup>1</sup>.

'''widdy'''<sup>1</sup>, '''widdie''' (wid′i), ''n.'' Dialectal forms of ''withy'', 3.

'''widdy'''<sup>2</sup> (wid′i), ''n.'' A dialectal form of ''widow''<sup>1</sup>.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
